beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about what a plan actually costs an AI agent. Today we are going to learn when breaking a task into steps is worth it, and when it is pure overhead. Most agent frameworks plan by default. Almost none of them ask whether planning is worth it for the task in front of them.

the ask types itself in, send button arms terracotta
running indicator: 'counting the calls…'
three output lines land: not free, halves the work, advantage disappears

props.command: When does planning a task up front actually pay for itself?
output: A plan is not free. It costs a call, and it commits you to a future you cannot see.
When nothing goes wrong, planning halves the work.
When something goes wrong early, the whole advantage disappears.

beats.act: ACT 1 — TWO WAYS TO DO A TASK
beats.narration_text: There are only two ways an agent can approach a task with several steps. Write the whole plan first, then run it. Or decide one step, run it, look at what happened, and decide again. Everything else is a blend of those two. The choice looks like a style preference. It is not. It is a bet.

beats.act: ACT 1 — TWO WAYS TO DO A TASK
beats.narration_text: So price them. An eight step task. Plan, then execute: one call to write the plan, eight to run it. Nine calls. Step by step: a call to decide and a call to act, every single step. Sixteen. Planning saves seven calls, which is close to half the work. That is a real advantage, and it is why frameworks default to it.

show.event: the plan-then-execute row writes on: 9 calls
the step-by-step row lands beneath it: 16 calls
the saving lands last: 7 calls

props.artifactTitle: planner.py — an eight step task, nothing goes wrong
props.artifactHeading: Planning halves the work. When it holds.

beats.narration_text: Here is the same task, with something going wrong at step k. Read the bottom row up. Fail at step eight and planning still wins comfortably. Fail at step four and the margin is thin. Fail at step one, and planning costs eighteen calls against eighteen. The entire advantage is gone, because all eight planned steps described a world that no longer exists.

show.event: the table writes on from k equals eight upward
the middle rows land, the margin visibly narrowing
the k equals one row lands: 18 against 18, eight steps discarded
the 'advantage is GONE' marker holds at the top

props.artifactTitle: planner.py — something goes wrong at step k
props.artifactHeading: The earlier the surprise, the less a plan was worth

beats.narration_text: So here is the rule, in plain terms. Plan when a wrong step is expensive to take back, when the ground is not moving under you, and when step four genuinely cannot happen before step three. Otherwise, do not plan. Just take one step and look. Looking is the cheapest information an agent can buy.

layers.title: Steps are expensive

layers.title: The world is stable

layers.title: Order genuinely matters
layers.sub: step four cannot happen before step three — the only thing a plan buys

props.caption: Miss any one of these and a plan is latency you paid for before learning anything.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. Planning is not free and it is not automatically smart. On an eight step task it saves seven model calls when nothing goes wrong, and that advantage shrinks the earlier reality diverges, reaching zero if the very first step surprises you. A plan earns its call only when steps are expensive, the world is stable, and order genuinely matters. All three, not two. And the most expensive pattern of all is a plan that gets written, displayed, and then ignored, because you pay for it twice and can audit neither.

props.artifactHeading: A plan is a bet that the world will hold still
artifactLines: Two strategies exist: plan then execute, or decide one step at a time. Everything else blends them.
On an 8 step task, planning costs 9 calls against 16. It halves the work when it holds.
A surprise at step 1 makes it 18 against 18. The earlier the divergence, the less the plan was worth.
Planning earns its call only when steps are expensive, the world is stable, AND order matters.
The costliest pattern is a plan that is written, shown, then ignored — paid for twice, auditable never.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Look at the agent I am building and tell me whether it plans. If it does, answer three things: how many steps it commits to before it looks at anything, what happens to those steps when step two fails, and whether any code actually reads the plan after step one. Then tell me if the plan is doing work or just being displayed. Run that against something you have built. The third question is the uncomfortable one, and it is usually the fastest thing you will fix all week.

output: Most planners commit to more steps than anyone has checked.

Watch Planning and Decomposition for the whole story. The link is right below. Adwait Changan, for Humanitarians AI.
